nodes.name: Regulated transmission and distribution utility rate base
nodes.mechanism: Utilities place new transmission, substation, and distribution assets into rate base, earning an allowed return on the incremental capital.
nodes.logic: The effect is levered because rate base additions compound under a regulated return while load growth from data centers provides a durable demand justification. Even a small increase in allowed capex translates directly into higher earnings from the allowed return on equity applied to the larger asset base.
nodes.falsifier: State commissions cap or disallow the data center-related capex in rate cases, preventing the assets from entering rate base.

nodes.name: High-voltage transformer, switchgear, and circuit breaker suppliers
nodes.mechanism: Utility procurement orders for power transformers, breakers, and switchgear push supplier backlogs to multi-year levels, allowing pricing to firm.
nodes.logic: Demand is levered to the scenario because long-lead grid equipment is a hard constraint: each new substation and transmission line requires multiple large power transformers and breakers, and supplier capacity is already tight. The resulting order book can exceed two years of production, shifting pricing power to manufacturers.
nodes.falsifier: Utilities cancel or reschedule orders because data center load does not sign or regulators deny the underlying projects.

nodes.name: Transmission and substation engineering and construction contractors
nodes.mechanism: Utilities award engineering, procurement, and construction contracts for new transmission lines, substations, and grid interconnections, expanding contractor backlog.
nodes.logic: The labor and specialized equipment required for transmission construction is scarce, so a given dollar of incremental capex translates into a larger share of project value captured by EPC firms through fixed-price and cost-plus contracts. Multi-year project timelines also provide revenue visibility beyond the initial order.
nodes.falsifier: Utilities self-perform more work or split projects into smaller packages that reduce individual contractor backlog.

nodes.name: Non-data-center commercial and industrial electricity customers
nodes.mechanism: Incremental grid capex is allocated through transmission and distribution rates, raising the per-MWh delivered cost for existing customers who do not add data center load.
nodes.logic: Regulators often allow utilities to recover capex through usage-based charges, so an increase in rate base without proportionate load growth from all customers raises rates for incumbents. The effect concentrates on energy-intensive industries whose margins are directly tied to electricity cost.
nodes.falsifier: Regulators assign data center-specific tariffs or direct assignment of costs to the new load, insulating existing customers from the increase.

nodes.name: Data center developers awaiting grid interconnection
nodes.mechanism: A surge of data center interconnection requests exceeds regional grid study and upgrade capacity, delaying energization timelines and increasing deposit and network upgrade costs.
nodes.logic: Interconnection queues already have multi-year study cycles, and the incremental load from data centers pushes queue volumes further beyond the available engineering and construction resources. The delay acts as a tax on data center development because schedule slippage extends time to revenue and raises the non-recurring network upgrade fees.
nodes.falsifier: FERC or grid operators adopt cluster study reforms or fast-track data center requests, clearing queue bottlenecks.

nodes.name: Utility rate case and prudence review exposure
nodes.mechanism: Regulators respond to the capex increase by tightening prudence reviews and cost recovery conditions, which can reduce allowed returns or defer recovery of project costs.
nodes.logic: As rate base requests rise, utilities face more aggressive intervention from ratepayer advocates and state commissions seeking to disallow speculative or over-budget projects. The effect is not linear because a single disallowance or cap can offset the earnings contribution from many approved projects.
nodes.falsifier: Commissions accept the data center load forecasts and pre-approve the projects, leaving little room for later disallowance.

nodes.name: High-voltage equipment manufacturing capacity and pricing
nodes.mechanism: Equipment suppliers respond to multi-year backlog by adding factory capacity and raising prices on new orders, increasing revenue and gross margin per unit.
nodes.logic: Because lead times for power transformers and breakers are already long, suppliers hold pricing power and can commit to capacity expansion only against visible multi-year contracts. The scenario converts a cyclical order spike into a longer pricing cycle as utilities accept higher prices to hold delivery slots.
nodes.falsifier: A wave of imports or new competitor capacity arrives before utilities place firm orders, causing suppliers to compete on price instead.

nodes.name: Behind-the-meter solar, storage, and energy efficiency providers
nodes.mechanism: Rising utility rates push commercial and industrial customers to contract for on-site solar, battery storage, and demand response, adding new customer-funded projects.
nodes.logic: When delivered electricity rates cross the levelized cost of distributed generation plus storage, the payback for behind-the-meter investment shortens, pulling forward discretionary energy projects. The effect is concentrated among customers with large flat load profiles and high demand charges.
nodes.falsifier: Utility rates do not rise enough to make behind-the-meter economics compelling, or customers remain locked into long-term utility supply contracts.

nodes.name: On-site and dedicated gas generation for data centers
nodes.mechanism: Data center operators facing multi-year grid interconnection delays contract for on-site gas turbines, reciprocating engines, and fuel cells, creating a direct equipment and service revenue stream.
nodes.logic: The response is driven by the opportunity cost of delay: data center revenue per MW is high enough to justify premium on-site generation even if grid power later becomes available. This creates a parallel demand channel for gas generation suppliers that is not dependent on utility procurement.
nodes.falsifier: Grid operators and utilities accelerate interconnection or data center developers accept longer timelines rather than pay for on-site generation.

nodes.name: High-voltage equipment suppliers face late-cycle overcapacity
nodes.mechanism: Supplier capacity additions and import responses eventually outpace remaining utility demand, causing lead times to shorten and prices to fall from peak.
nodes.logic: The scenario pulls forward a large amount of equipment demand, and suppliers who expand capacity based on peak order rates can overshoot when the initial wave is installed. The resulting competitive pricing erodes the gross margin gains that attracted the capacity in the first place.
nodes.falsifier: Demand remains strong beyond 2030 because data center load is understated or additional grid replacement demand absorbs the new capacity.

nodes.name: Regulated utility revenue erosion from customer self-supply
nodes.mechanism: As C&I customers self-supply a growing share of power, utility billed volume growth weakens and the fixed cost of the expanded grid is spread over fewer remaining kWh, raising rates further for remaining customers.
nodes.logic: The dynamic is self-reinforcing: each cohort of customers defecting to distributed generation raises rates for those left, which makes the next cohort's economics more attractive. Utilities with high capex relative to delivered volume face the sharpest decline in throughput.
nodes.falsifier: Data center load growth offsets defection and utilities retain C&I customers through special tariffs or load retention programs.

nodes.name: Gas turbine and engine service and aftermarket providers
nodes.mechanism: The installed base of on-site data center gas generation creates long-term service, parts, and overhaul revenue tied to operating hours and maintenance schedules.
nodes.logic: Because data center operators run on-site generation as primary or peaking power, engines accumulate run hours faster than standby units, pulling maintenance intervals forward. The aftermarket is higher margin and more recurring than the original equipment sale.
nodes.falsifier: Data centers switch to grid power as soon as interconnection arrives, leaving on-site units as rarely used backup with minimal aftermarket.

trigger.actor: US regulated utilities and transmission owners, with data center developers as anchor customers
trigger.action: commit to a multi-year acceleration of grid transmission, distribution, and substation capital expenditures
trigger.magnitude: annual US grid capex rises by roughly $40 billion to $60 billion above the 2025 baseline by 2030, supporting an incremental 30 to 50 GW of data center load
trigger.geography: United States, concentrated in PJM, ERCOT, Southeast, and Southwest markets
trigger.timing: 2026 to 2030, with orders and rate cases starting in 2025 and construction peaking in 2028 to 2030
trigger.certainty: assumed; several utility plans are announced but depend on signed data center load contracts and regulatory approval
trigger.reversibility: utilities can defer or cancel project tranches if data center load fails to materialize or regulators disallow cost recovery

reactions.incentive: maximize allowed return on rate base
reactions.likelyResponse: file advanced rate cases and front-load transmission and substation projects, ordering long-lead equipment

reactions.incentive: secure large power blocks quickly and avoid cost and schedule risk
reactions.likelyResponse: sign long-term take-or-pay contracts, pay for dedicated substations, and evaluate on-site generation where queues stall

reactions.incentive: ensure reliability while protecting ratepayers from overpaying for speculative load
reactions.likelyResponse: require demand-based cost allocation, prudence reviews, and cost caps or clawbacks

reactions.incentive: capture multi-year demand and maximize margins
reactions.likelyResponse: expand manufacturing capacity, raise prices, lengthen lead times, and prefer standardized large orders

reactions.actor: Existing commercial and industrial electricity customers
reactions.incentive: avoid higher rates and supply constraints
reactions.likelyResponse: intervene against rate increases and invest in behind-the-meter generation, storage, and efficiency
